nameStory: The Common Buckeye gets its name from the striking eyespots on its wings that resemble the glossy brown seeds of buckeye trees. These bold, circular markings with their dark centers surrounded by lighter rings look just like the 'buck's eye' that gave buckeye trees their name. It's a perfect case of nature's patterns appearing in completely different places!
description: The Common Buckeye is a medium-sized butterfly with distinctive large eyespots that make it unmistakable in flight. Its wings are primarily brown and tan with prominent circular eyespots - typically two large ones on the hindwings and smaller ones on the forewings. The butterfly has a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and belongs to the brush-footed butterfly family, meaning its front legs are reduced and brush-like. You'll often see them flying low and fast over open ground, landing frequently to bask in sunny spots.

idTips.label: Eyespots
idTips.description: Large, bold circular eyespots with dark centers and light rings - two prominent ones on each hindwing and smaller ones on forewings that flash dramatically when wings open

idTips.label: Wing Color
idTips.description: Rich brown and tan coloration with lighter bands crossing the forewings, creating an earthy, mottled appearance

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Fast, low flight with frequent stops to bask on bare ground or rocks with wings spread wide to catch the sun's warmth

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized butterfly with wingspan of 2-3 inches - noticeably larger than a skipper but smaller than a swallowtail

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Forewings are somewhat triangular and pointed, hindwings are rounded with scalloped edges that feel papery-thin to the touch

habitat: Common Buckeyes prefer open, sunny areas with low vegetation and patches of bare ground where they can easily spot predators and bask in the sun. Look for them in fields, meadows, roadsides, gardens, and disturbed areas like construction sites or vacant lots. They particularly favor areas where their host plants - plantains, snapdragons, and other low-growing herbs - are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring as migrants move north from southern wintering areas. Look for fresh individuals with bright, unmarked wing patterns.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs in summer with multiple generations flying. Adults are most active on warm, sunny days and can be seen nectaring on flowers throughout the day.
seasonality.fall: Fall brings the largest populations as northern-born butterflies migrate south. Wings may show wear from travel, making eyespots appear faded or damaged.
seasonality.winter: Not present in New England winters - these butterflies migrate south to warmer climates where they cannot survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Common Buckeye caterpillars seek out plants that produce bitter compounds called iridoid glycosides, which make the caterpillars taste terrible to predators like ants and birds - essentially turning them into living chemical weapons that most predators will spit out rather than eat!
confusionNotes: The large eyespots make Common Buckeyes nearly impossible to confuse with other New England butterflies. The closest might be some moths with eyespots, but buckeyes fly during the day while most eyespot moths are nocturnal. Remember: if you see prominent eyespots on a day-flying butterfly, it's almost certainly a buckeye.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Common' Buckeye, this species is actually somewhat uncommon in northern New England and more frequently seen in southern portions of the region. They're strong migrants that can't survive New England winters, so all individuals you see have either flown north from southern states or are descendants of migrants.
compareHints: The Common Buckeye is the only member of its genus regularly found in New England, making identification straightforward. Within the brush-footed butterfly family, its large eyespots immediately distinguish it from relatives like painted ladies (which have smaller, less prominent eyespots) or mourning cloaks (which are much darker with yellow wing borders). No other New England butterfly has such bold, buckeye-seed-like eyespots.
